title: Hear the Driver
concept: After this one you can hear which Must is running in a short clip by reading the words and the hands together, even when they disagree.
bookIdea: Drivers are five Musts (be perfect, please others, try hard, be strong, hurry up), each a condition for feeling OK, and each shows in a person's words, tone and body.

opener.setting: Wednesday, 7:05am. Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B, the kitchen. The cab is due at 7:15.

lines.text: “Quick, quick, the cab's here. Grab the bag, I'll explain on the way.”
lines.cue: one shoe on, the other in his hand

lines.text: “It's fine. Go. Don't worry about the bins, I'll do them.”
lines.cue: already at the sink, back to the room

opener.ask: Name the Must behind each short clip. Sometimes the words and the hands disagree, so check both.

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Each clip lasts a few seconds: what someone says, and what their hands and face do. Name the Must it runs on. The five Musts are be perfect, please others, try hard, be strong and hurry up.

items.text: “Two commas. Fix them before it goes out.”
items.cue: reading the email a second time, pen clicking on each comma
items.why: The words are about small errors, and the pen goes over each comma again. The Must is be perfect: nothing is allowed to slip, and a clean page is the only way to feel OK.

traps.1: It would sound like “Whatever you think is best, go ahead.” Nothing in the clip is about being liked. The team would hear a boss who has stopped checking and is handing the email over.
traps.2: It would sound like “Quick, send it, we're late.” The pen stops on every comma, though. The speed would tell the team the checks don't matter, and the one check he needs would be skipped.

items.example: A cricket club scorer, Saturday. He recounts the same over three times while the batsmen wait: “One more look. The total has to be exact.”

items.text: “It's fine, sit, sit. I'll do the dishes. You take the chair, I've eaten.”
items.cue: already at the sink, back to the room, not turning round
items.why: Every line is about being no bother: it's fine, you sit, I've eaten. The Must is please others, and the dishes are the price of being easy to be around.

traps.0: It would sound like “I'll get it right this time, just give me a minute.” The clip shows no effort. She is not trying to get something right, she is trying not to be any trouble.
traps.2: It would sound like “I don't need a chair, I'm fine standing.” That refuses help, and this clip is the opposite. She is giving the chair away to make him comfortable.

items.example: A bank queue, Tuesday. A man lets a woman with a baby go first, then waves off her thanks: “No, no, it's nothing. After you.” He has waited forty minutes, and his own form is still wrong.

items.text: “Okay, okay, I'm ready. Where are my keys? Quick, quick, the cab's already here.”
items.cue: keys in his teeth, jacket half on, checking the microwave clock
items.why: The clock is in his eyes, and the word 'quick' comes twice in one line. The Must is hurry up: the day is a race he is already losing, so he rushes the next step before he knows what it is.

traps.1: It would sound like “I'll get there, I'm trying, give me a minute.” Nothing in the clip shows effort, only speed. The cabbie would hear someone who is trying, when what he needs is a plan.
traps.2: It would sound like “Wait, let me check the bag. Did I lock the door?” That is a careful clip, and Sam is skipping checks. Nothing is being perfected here, only hurried through.

items.example: A train platform, 6:58am. A mother runs for a carriage with a child on her hip. She keeps saying “Come on, come on” to a child who is still tying a shoelace.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: These clips are harder. The words and the hands point in different directions, and the options look alike. Listen to both, then ask which one the person is holding on to.

items.text: “I'm fine, really. It's just the same cell. I'm trying, I'll have it in a minute.”
items.cue: the spreadsheet opened for the fourth time, brow tight, nose almost on the screen
items.why: The words say fine, and the body says effort. The same cell, opened again and again, is what try hard looks like: the trying is the point, and it never reaches the finish. The 'I'm fine' is the cover.

traps.0: It would sound like “I'm fine, I'll sort it myself.” Her teammates would believe the words, so nobody would offer to look at the cell with her, and the fourth opening would go on alone.
traps.2: It would sound like “Just one more check, the cell has to be exact.” That is a real Must, but this clip isn't about exactness. Nothing is being checked for errors. It is pushed for a result that doesn't come.
traps.3: It would sound like “Take your time, I don't mind waiting.” Her eyes are on the cell and nowhere near anyone else's comfort.

items.example: A family WhatsApp group for a wedding: “I'm fine, really, I'll sort the venue tomorrow.” At midnight she posts the fourth draft of the same menu card.

items.text: “Whatever's easiest for everyone. I'm fine doing it, really.”
items.cue: carrying the crate alone, arms locked, waving off the trolley someone holds out
items.why: The words sound like a gift to everyone: whatever's easiest. The hands say the opposite. He will not let anyone share the load, and that is be strong, the Must that says needing help is a weakness.

traps.0: It would sound like “Let me think, what would suit everyone?” That is please others, and the clip doesn't ask the room what suits it. The crate would stay on his back and nobody would know he was struggling.
traps.2: It would sound like “Give me a minute, I'll get the hang of this crate.” It has the look of effort, but Omar is not trying to master the crate. He is refusing the trolley and the hand.

items.example: A grandfather at a family wedding carries every bag from the car and turns down his nephew: “I've carried worse. Go and sit down.”

items.text: “Maya says 'it's fine' and 'sit, sit' before breakfast, then takes the dishes. Which explanation fits best?”
items.cue: sliding her cup across the table to the empty seat
options: She runs be strong: she handles everything alone so no one has to be bothered.
She runs please others: the 'it's fine' is the Must, and the dishes keep her from being any trouble.
She runs hurry up: the dishes get done fast so the morning moves.
items.why: The books call these drivers, and this one is please others. Every line is about not being a bother: it's fine, sit, I've eaten. Be strong would have refused the chair outright, and hurry up would have talked about the clock.

traps.0: Sam would take her at her word and say “Great, see you.” Nobody would ask whether she had eaten, and the cover would be read as strength.
traps.2: The talk would turn to time, and the lines about the chair would be put down to nerves. Maya's real pull is being no trouble, and it would stay hidden under a joke about the clock.

items.example: A school gate, Monday. A mother says “It's fine, I'll wait,” and holds three other parents' bags while her own son is called in late.

debrief.nadia: Five Musts, and each one can pass for a good habit at first. Listen for the word that gets said too often, then check whether the hands agree. The clip that fooled you was probably the one where the words were kind.
debrief.bookNote: The books call these drivers: five Musts, each a condition for feeling OK, that show in a person's words, tone and body.

reflection.prompt: Which Must did you hear yourself running this week, and what were your hands doing just before?
